title: Antibiotic Treatment for 7 versus 14 Days in Patients with Bloodstream Infections
shortTitle: BALANCE: seven days for selected bloodstream infections
authors: BALANCE Investigators, for the Canadian Critical Care Trials Group, the Association of Medical Microbiology and Infectious Disease Canada Clinical Research Network, the Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society Clinical Trials Group, and the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases Clinical Research Network

The BALANCE Investigators, for the Canadian Critical Care Trials Group, the Association of Medical Microbiology and Infectious Disease Canada Clinical Research Network, the Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society Clinical Trials Group, and the Australasian Society for Infectious Diseases Clinical Research Network
summary: BALANCE randomized 3,608 hospitalized patients with bloodstream infection to 7 or 14 days of antibiotics. Ninety-day mortality was 14.5% versus 16.1% (difference −1.6 percentage points; 95.7% CI −4.0 to 0.8), meeting the prespecified 4-point noninferiority margin. More than half were in an ICU at enrollment.
whyItMatters: Supports avoiding an automatic 14-day course for eligible bacteremia once the pathogen, source and clinical course are established. It does not justify shorter treatment for excluded infections.
limitations: Severe immunosuppression, S aureus bacteremia and foci requiring prolonged therapy were excluded. Treatment exceeded assignment in 23.1% of the 7-day group; noninferiority is not proof that all durations are equivalent.
population: Hospitalized adults with bloodstream infection at 74 hospitals in seven countries.
intervention: Seven days of antibiotics; agent, dose and route selected clinically.
primaryEndpoint: All-cause mortality by 90 days after bloodstream infection diagnosis.
findings: Per-protocol risk difference: −2.0 percentage points (95% CI −4.5 to 0.6).
evidenceNotes: Historical backfill: first-online date verified from the PubMed electronic publication record. Abstract reviewed; full text unavailable. This is historical evidence, not a new 2026 publication.
